articles.body:
For all its green-washing, the Zionist state has ecologically devastated Palestine more than anyone else.

A month into this year’s olive harvest season, Israeli settlers and soldiers have already damaged or uprooted 4,500 olive trees in the occupied West Bank. Since January, they have destroyed 100,000 olive trees. In Gaza, since October 2023, 97 percent of Gaza’s two million olive oil trees have been wiped out. Between 1967, when Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, and the 2010s, it had destroyed more than 800,000.

I think of the devastating sight of uprooted trees in my grandfather’s olive grove every time I hear news of Israel sending yet another delegation to a climate, biodiversity, or desertification conference to boast of its “unique expertise” in “making the desert bloom” – a myth it has long propagated.

The destruction of olive trees is just one aspect of Israel’s broader war on the Palestinian land, from its vegetation and soil to its water and ecosystems. Since the Nakba of 1948, Israeli colonial policies have extended beyond land seizure and the displacement of its inhabitants to reshaping the natural landscape, undermining its capacity to sustain those who have lived on and cultivated it for generations.

In other words, contrary to its greenwashing claims, Israel made a blooming Palestine burn.

Re-engineering ‘the desert’

When the first Zionist settlers started coming to Palestine in the late 19th century, what they found was “a desert” that was already blooming. Palestinian land was producing not only enough food to feed its people but also to export to neighbouring regions within the Ottoman Empire and even across the Mediterranean to Europe.

Palestinians were growing wheat, barley and oats and harvesting olive and fruit trees. Closer to the Mediterranean coast, lush gardens produced various vegetables and fruit. In the more arid Naqab desert in the south, Bedouin tribes tended to herds of sheep, goats and camels, producing meat, milk and wool.

Palestinians co-existed with the various ecosystems they occupied: from wetlands to the dry desert. They tended to the land using techniques that reflected local conditions rather than seeking to engineer them. Local drought-resistant crops were grown in drier areas and more irrigation-dependent ones in valleys closer to water sources.

By contrast, Zionist settlers coming from Europe sought to reshape Palestine’s landscape to what was familiar to them. They planted trees imported from Europe, such as the stone pine, in some cases uprooting native species, including olive trees. They drained swamps, rerouted streams and tried to afforest desert landscapes.

Some of these activities had disastrous consequences for local ecosystems, including the introduction of non-native plants such as the eucalyptus, which burns easily and which has contributed to a higher frequency and intensity of wildfires.

Israel’s efforts to reshape the natural landscape were driven by the desire to erase Palestinian presence. Trees were planted over the remains of pillaged Palestinian villages to cover them up. Imported European-style agriculture wiped out native Palestinian techniques that had produced food for centuries.

Ecocide in Palestine

The Zionist assault on the Palestinian land did not stop at the 1948 boundaries. As soon as the Israeli army occupied the West Bank and Gaza, it put under martial rule not just the people but also their natural resources.

Water has been at the centre of this process. As illegal settlements spread in the occupied territories, settlers started taking over local water resources. Today, Israel’s national water company, Mekorot, is responsible for running an extensive water system that reroutes water from Palestinian towns and villages to the Israeli settlements. It often cuts off water to Palestinians in the summer to ensure a steady supply to the illegal settlers.

This water theft has devastated Palestinian agriculture and ecosystems.

Meanwhile, land theft has featured not only violence against the Palestinian people but also against their soil. For years, the Israeli army and settlers have sprayed Palestinian land with pesticides to discourage farmers from working their fields. Meanwhile, burning and uprooting of trees and other vegetation, as well as settler construction, have damaged the soil and led to erosion.

In Gaza, ecocide has been taken to the extreme. The genocidal war unleashed on the Gaza Strip has devastated agricultural land, trees, soil and water.

These harms are compounded by bombardment and bulldozing. Israel has destroyed approximately 85 percent of buildings in the Gaza Strip, leaving an estimated 70 million tonnes of rubble containing various toxins. Israeli bombardment has dispersed heavy metals, including lead, cadmium, arsenic, tungsten and aluminium, as well as explosive compounds such as TNT, RDX and perchlorates.

These substances seep into the soil and groundwater, causing environmental damage whose effects may persist for years.

Meanwhile, the continuing bulldozing of buildings and land has stripped away the topsoil, which is rich in organic matter and nutrients essential for plant growth, further degrading agricultural land.

A coloniser’s logic

The paradox here is that the Israelis who claim to have an ancient right to the land are the very same people who damage and destroy it. This is highly surprising.

A coloniser sees land as something to capture, possess and exploit. The colonial relationship to land is one of abuse for the sake of material benefit. It is not care. It is not stewardship. It is not belonging.

The Israeli approach to Palestinian land – poison and destroy in order to control – contrasts sharply with the Palestinian one. Since 1948, Palestinians have faced constant attacks, destruction, theft of resources, pillaging. And yet, they have sought to rebuild, replant and rework over and over again.

My own grandfather, Hamdan, is an example of this Palestinian spirit. For four decades he looked over an eight-dunam olive grove that produced 1,500kg of olive oil each season.

During the 2008 war, the Israeli army bulldozed the grove. My grandfather did not relent. He replanted olive trees with my help. Just as the grove was beginning to recover, the Israeli army destroyed it again during the 2014 war.

For my grandfather, the olive trees were more than a livelihood. He saw them as his children, the fruit of years of care and his family’s bond to the land. Less than a week after their destruction in 2014, my grandfather died from the shock.

We did not relent either. My family set out to restore and replant the land with olive trees in 2015, which took several months. The trees then took three years to bear fruit. We managed to harvest olives for two seasons before the Israeli army bombed the grove during the 2021 war.

The land was so damaged that it was no longer suitable for olive cultivation. Clearing the contamination and burying the bomb craters took a long time, but we still managed to plant some of the land with seasonal crops like wheat. Then in December 2023, the Israeli army devastated the grove again.

I would be replanting that land again today if it didn’t lie beyond the ever-expanding “Yellow Line”.

That drive to tend to land is so deeply ingrained in Palestinians that even in the camps for the displaced, people are keeping small gardens in front of their tents, planting mint, basil and flowers.

Despite all the propaganda and greenwashing Israel deploys, it is increasingly clear to the world who can make the Holy Land bloom. It is not those who destroy, poison and bulldoze. It is those who are deeply rooted, who plant, grow and care. Those are the true owners of the land.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
articles.summary: Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group. "In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects. The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babylon province, an interior ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the oil ministry. Numan did not elaborate on the role of the sacked officials in the alleged smuggling operations. A committee investigating the allegations entered Jurf al-Sakher on Friday, accompanied by members of Kataeb Hezbollah. On Wednesday, the state news agency INA reported that "intelligence documents" containing satellite images "showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction" in Jurf al-Sakher, accusing the unnamed faction of tapping into a pipeline there. According to Numan, the investigating committee "confirmed the accuracy" of the information. Report by AFP

articles.title: Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
articles.summary: China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage.
articles.preview: November 15, 2026 China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage. An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week. China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place.
articles.body:
November 15, 2026

China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image on the global stage.

An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen this week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.

End of campaign to isolate Putin?

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.

"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.

She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.

"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.

Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership

Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.

At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.

China helping Russia from the sidelines

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.

While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.

Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.

What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis?

In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.

China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.

China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war

But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.

Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.

"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

articles.title: “El idilio de los medios con Trump ha acabado”: la victoria demócrata cambia las reglas de la prensa de Washington
articles.summary: La debilidad del presidente tras el revés de las ‘midterms’ reabre el debate sobre cómo cubrir a un político que se nutre de la atención de una profesión a la que ataca constantemente
articles.preview: La debilidad del presidente tras el revés de las ‘midterms’ reabre el debate sobre cómo cubrir a un político que se nutre de la atención de una profesión a la que ataca constantemente La prensa de Washington lleva más de una década enganchada a una droga conocida en el mercado negro de las noticias como el Trump Bump (algo así como el Subidón Trump).
articles.body:
La debilidad del presidente tras el revés de las ‘midterms’ reabre el debate sobre cómo cubrir a un político que se nutre de la atención de una profesión a la que ataca constantemente

La prensa de Washington lleva más de una década enganchada a una droga conocida en el mercado negro de las noticias como el Trump Bump (algo así como el Subidón Trump). Tiene (o tenía) efectos inmediatos sobre la audiencia de los medios, y dispara (o disparaba) la relevancia de estos en la eterna pelea por la atención a base de hablar incesantemente del presidente de Estados Unidos. Es barata, se produce en cantidades industriales y provoca adicción. También, ese cierto remordimiento que dejan las gratificaciones inmediatas.

Pero hace algún tiempo que sus efectos no son tan poderosos como solían. Casi dos años después de la vuelta de Trump al poder, sus mentiras, ataques al decoro y ocurrencias para frotarse los ojos han hecho perder fuerza a la capacidad de enganche del inquilino de la Casa Blanca más heterodoxo. Tras la histórica derrota republicana de la semana pasada en las elecciones de mitad de mandato, la pregunta en la prensa tradicional estadounidense es si los electores, además de propinar un revés al presidente, no habrán querido enviar el mensaje de que ya tuvieron suficiente de esa droga.

“El idilio de los medios con Trump ha acabado”, considera en una entrevista telefónica la profesora de periodismo de la Universidad de Columbia Margaret Sullivan, que fue defensora del lector de The New York Times y redactora de medios en The Washington Post. “Hasta Fox News, su mayor valedora, ha reducido la cobertura constante sobre él”, añade. Sullivan habla de una caída de la audiencia reconocida por el propio Lachlan Murdoch, heredero del imperio de su padre, Rupert Murdoch, en una conferencia con inversores el pasado 2 de noviembre, víspera de las midterms. Murdoch atribuyó a la “fatiga de los televidentes” el mal dato en la cadena de noticias más vista.

Lo cual podría significar que por una vez el jefe de Fox News está de acuerdo en algo con Jeff Jarvis, una de las voces más críticas del periodismo estadounidense. “La gente lleva exhausta demasiado tiempo. Su vuelta a la Casa Blanca pudo reverdecer algo el interés [de la audiencia] en él, pero solo sirvió para que descubriéramos la dimensión de nuestro hartazgo. El síndrome de abstinencia ya pasó”, explica en una videoconferencia este profesor emérito de la Universidad de la Ciudad de Nueva York (CUNY).

Los ataques a la prensa han sido una constante desde que Trump regresó al poder a principios de 2025. El presidente de Estados Unidos ha demandado al Times o a The Wall Street Journal y ha amenazado a televisiones con la retirada de licencias televisivas como represalia por una supuesta cobertura negativa. Ha vetado el acceso de cabeceras a la Casa Blanca, pero, sobre todo, ha contribuido a derechizar el paisaje mediático con la ayuda de aliados como Elon Musk, propietario de X; Jeff Bezos, dueño de un degradado Washington Post; y Larry y David Ellison. La Administración autorizó a estos últimos la fusión de Paramount y Skydance. Los Ellison, padre e hijo, controlan una fortuna con fuertes intereses en Hollywood. Larry Ellison, fundador de Oracle, es además amigo personal de Trump.

Esa operación puso en la órbita de los ideales MAGA (el movimiento trumpista Make America Great Again) a la división de noticias de la venerable CBS, ahora bajo el mando de la periodista antiwoke Bari Weiss. Esta anda empeñada en llevar la emisora a la derecha con, de momento, malos resultados de audiencia y en términos de prestigio en la profesión.

Entrevistas ‘post mortem’

El hecho de que Trump escogiera uno de los programas más intervenidos por Weiss, 60 Minutes, como el lugar para dar su primera entrevista-autopsia tras la derrota en las midterms dice mucho de cuánto han cambiado las cosas: se trata del mismo espacio al que el entonces candidato no quiso acudir en la campaña de 2024. Tras la cita con las urnas de la semana pasada, el presidente de Estados Unidos se ha sentado otras dos veces más con la prensa para hablar en detalle: con el muy leal locutor radiofónico Hugh Hewitt y con el comentarista deportivo Stephen A. Smith (ESPN).

En la cartera de los Ellison, cuyo patriarca fundó Oracle y es amigo personal de Trump, también figura desde el mes pasado CNN, gracias, de nuevo, a la fusión tolerada por la Casa Blanca. La cadena de televisión por cable lleva años en crisis, pero, pese a la menguante audiencia, mantiene su influencia en Washington.

Antes de las midterms, sus periodistas ―que, como los de MS NOW, más a la izquierda, presentaron con entusiasmo las noticias de la debacle electoral republicana― temían un giro parecido al de CBS News. Ahora que la capital estadounidense ha dado la bienvenida a una nueva era de mayorías demócratas en el Capitolio, la pregunta es si a los Ellison les moverán las motivaciones ideológicas o lo que sea mejor para el negocio en una realidad en la que la invencibilidad de Trump y el mundo MAGA no es la que era.

Tampoco entre sus fieles: una investigación de The Wall Street Journal concluyó en septiembre, gracias a un rastreo con IA de 70.000 horas de podcasts MAGA, que las menciones por hora al presidente han caído estrepitosamente en los últimos meses, especialmente desde el inicio de la guerra de Irán. De momento, la nueva propiedad de CNN ha avisado de que no relevará a su consejero delegado, el respetado Mark Thompson, aunque en esa decisión, como analiza una empleada de CNN que prefiere no dar su nombre, tal vez haya pesado el hecho de que este ande cerca de la jubilación, a sus 69 años.

Mientras Fox News da tímidas señales de distanciamiento con Trump, un distanciamiento que ya ensayó Murdoch en 2021 −fue tras el asalto al Capitolio y antes de volver por conveniencia a los brazos MAGA− a los así llamados medios tradicionales −acosados por la caída de tráfico alentada por el declive de las redes sociales y por los cambios en los motores y hábitos de búsqueda digital que ha traído la inteligencia artificial− les va a costar cambiar los términos de su relación con un presidente al que les sigue uniendo una relación de dependencia mutua. Aquel odia a la prensa, pero vive pendiente de ella, mientras esta sigue sin haber dado con la fórmula que concilie el reto de informar sobre el inquilino de la Casa Blanca más mentiroso de la historia reciente con la obligación de atender a lo que dice, porque, después de todo, es el presidente de Estados Unidos.

Ni Sullivan ni Jarvis tienen demasiada fe en que los medios de Washington vayan a cambiar su estrategia a lomos del “tsunami azul [demócrata]” que salió de las urnas. “La prensa tradicional seguirá haciendo lo que ha venido haciendo: intentar mantener una postura neutral, procurar no ofender demasiado a nadie”, dice Sullivan.

Jarvis va más lejos: “Medios como el Post o el Times [del que este profesor es un duro crítico en X, con el hashtag #brokentimes] seguirán informando sin reconocer que el fascismo no es que esté a las puertas; es que ya entró en casa. Sus editores te dirán que solo es un adjetivo, cuando es un sustantivo con historia. Perseverarán en los eufemismos y la equidistancia. Cuando tratas a ambos lados por igual pero uno de ellos, la derecha, se ha ido al extremo, el resultado es que toda la discusión se mueve hacia ese lado”.

Ambos concuerdan también en que los movimientos de Trump tras la derrota ―del nombramiento del radical Stephen Miller como su hombre de confianza en la Casa Blanca al cierre de filas en torno al secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth― indican que el presidente no está dispuesto a aflojar su confrontación con aquellos que percibe como sus enemigos. Es una lista que encabezan los demócratas y la prensa tradicional, a la que lleva más de una década describiendo con aparente éxito como el “enemigo del pueblo”: solo un 32% de los estadounidenses se fía de los medios, según Gallup (cifra que, al menos, supone un ligero repunte con respecto al año pasado, cuando esta tocó suelo con un 28%).

Los demócratas han prometido usar su histórica victoria y sus amplias mayorías por estrenar en ambas cámaras para combatir a Miller, echar a Hegseth con un impeachment (juicio político), cuyo primer intento fracasó esta semana, y juzgar la presunta corrupción de la familia y la Administración de Trump. También tendrán en su mano la opción de plantar cara al desguace de los medios públicos por parte del Gobierno.

En el caso de la radio NPR y la televisión PBS, a cuya financiación Trump restó 1.100 millones de dólares, será difícil. Necesitan una mayoría de dos terceras partes en ambas cámaras para neutralizar el veto presidencial de la que carecen por sí mismos.

También está el caso de Voice of America (VOA), servicio exterior gubernamental de noticias que Elon Musk y su Departamento de Eficiencia Gubernamental (DOGE) puso en el punto de mira al principio de esta legislatura entre acusaciones de partidismo. Un millar de funcionarios federales despedidos en aquellos meses siguen en un limbo: aún cobran sus sueldos mientras esperan una resolución definitiva del litigio que mantienen con la Administración y un juez tras otro les da la razón.

El último tribunal en hacerlo ha sido esta semana el de apelaciones de Washington, que refrendó por unanimidad la decisión de una instancia inferior que consideró ilegal en marzo pasado los despidos de esos trabajadores y ordenó que el director de VOA, Michael Abramowitz, regresase a su puesto. El Congreso podría, además, renovar la financiación de un servicio de noticias fundado en 1942 para combatir el nazismo.

El siguiente episodio de ese culebrón tendrá como escenario la semana próxima el Senado, con la audiencia de confirmación de Sarah Rogers, la persona nombrada por Trump para liderar el desmantelamiento de VOA. Entre tanto, siete de sus filiales, que dan noticias en idiomas como el farsi, el urdu o el ucranio, han vuelto al trabajo, y algunos empleados han sido readmitidos.

El resto, tres de los cuales hablaron esta semana con EL PAÍS con la condición de hacerlo anónimamente, siguen a la espera para decidir si les compensa volver o si aceptan un despido definitivo. Todo dependerá, dijo uno de ellos, de si los vuelven a contratar “para hacer su trabajo o para dedicarse a la propaganda”, la clase de periodismo que mejor tolera Trump.

articles.title: Miriam Nogueras, candidata de Junts: “No me presento para poner o quitar presidentes españoles”
articles.summary: La cabeza de lista de la formación reivindica los éxitos que le ha dado la presión a Pedro Sánchez, pero veta al actual presidente para una eventual reelección
articles.preview: La cabeza de lista de la formación reivindica los éxitos que le ha dado la presión a Pedro Sánchez, pero veta al actual presidente para una eventual reelección La candidata de Junts per Catalunya para el 29-N gestiona la campaña aplicando las dotes que ha perfeccionado en sus clases de boxeo: prudencia al hablar para esquivar embestidas que pueden hacerla tambalear y, luego, golpear cuando ve la guardia baja.
articles.body:
La cabeza de lista de la formación reivindica los éxitos que le ha dado la presión a Pedro Sánchez, pero veta al actual presidente para una eventual reelección

La candidata de Junts per Catalunya para el 29-N gestiona la campaña aplicando las dotes que ha perfeccionado en sus clases de boxeo: prudencia al hablar para esquivar embestidas que pueden hacerla tambalear y, luego, golpear cuando ve la guardia baja. Es un valor al alza dentro del partido que comanda Carles Puigdemont y su empeño en reiterar que el expresident es el mejor líder posible no disipa los rumores que la sitúan al frente de la lista de sustitutos si, una vez haya regresado a Cataluña, Puigdemont decide dar un paso al lado.

Pregunta. ¿El resultado de las elecciones ya está decidido o la campaña puede alterar los presagios de las encuestas?

Respuesta. Confío en que nos sirva de altavoz para explicar lo que ya hemos expuesto durante toda la legislatura, todo el trabajo que hemos hecho y el rigor que hemos aplicado. Junts es el único partido que, sin estar en el Gobierno, ha logrado aprobar leyes propias.

P. Carles Puigdemont, presidente de su partido, dice que regresará tras el 29-N. ¿Cree que el resultado para Junts podría ser mejor si lo tuviera a su lado durante la campaña?

R. Es que ya lo tengo a mi lado. Siempre lo ha estado. Regresará cuando tenga que regresar y cómo él crea que tiene que regresar.

P. Al cerrar el escrutinio de la noche electoral, ¿con qué escenario se sentiría más cómodo Junts?

R. Sin duda, con un resultado que nos dé mucha fuerza y que garantice que en Madrid no se pueda tomar ni una decisión sin contar con Cataluña.

P. ¿Que Cataluña tenga más fuerza también implica que a ERC le vayan bien las cosas?

R. El problema es que algunos partidos han preferido meterse dentro del bloque de partidos españoles, y fuera de ese bloque solo está Junts per Catalunya.

P. La rivalidad natural entre Junts y ERC va bastante más allá cuando el enfrentamiento es entre Nogueras y Rufián. ¿Le dolería especialmente sacar peor resultado que él?

R. No voy a estar pendiente del ruido y de los insultos. El señor Rufián ha estado ocho años haciendo de muleta del PSOE y, lamentablemente, su partido no ha podido impulsar ni una sola ley propia. En los dos años y medio que duró el acuerdo de Junts con los socialistas, logramos rebajar impuestos, un ahorro de 10.000 millones de euros para las pymes catalanas y 20 millones para los 21.000 clubes deportivos de Cataluña. En Junts no somos influencers, nuestra responsabilidad es hacer que la vida de las personas sea un poco mejor cada día.

P. Si han sacado réditos de la negociación con el PSOE, ¿no cuesta explicar que rompieran relaciones con el Gobierno?

R. Quien decidió romper fue el Partido Socialista al no cumplir los acuerdos. Ojalá los hubiera cumplido y hubiéramos podido arrancar la ley contra las ocupaciones, que permanece en el cajón, o rebajar el IVA para dar aire a las familias, a los autónomos y a las pymes.

P. ¿Junts ve más posible poder cerrar acuerdos con un Gobierno del PSOE o con uno del PP?

R. Tenemos clarísimo lo que queremos, y lo vamos a defender delante de quien sea. Veremos qué sale el 29-N, pero en 2023 ya elegimos dejar fuera a PP-Vox. El PP ganó las elecciones y no ha gobernado gracias a Junts. Ahora bien, el PSOE tendrá que decidir si prioriza al señor Sánchez o si prioriza al partido y al país que dice defender.

P. ¿Junts no investirá a Pedro Sánchez?

R. Sánchez lleva ocho años gobernando España y las decisiones que ha tomado y las políticas que ha aplicado no han hecho al país mejor, no han ayudado a las personas a tener una vida mejor. El coste de la vida es altísimo y en el terreno de la vivienda ha resultado ser un desastre, con menos oferta que nunca y los precios más altos. España es de los países de la UE que menos invierte en vivienda pública. Ha demostrado que no tiene la capacidad de sacar adelante ni los acuerdos ni los consensos.

P. ¿Junts vería con mejores ojos una investidura de Feijóo sin Vox antes que volver a darle la presidencia a Pedro Sánchez?

R. El PP está absolutamente secuestrado por Vox. La catalanofobia que desprende es total. La cuestión no es si nos sentimos más cómodos con los unos o con los otros, el tema es que lo mejor que le puede pasar a Cataluña hasta que no sea un Estado es que en Madrid todo dependa de Cataluña. Y solo Junts puede garantizar que la agenda catalana estará en el centro. Lo que pase a partir del 29-N no es mi responsabilidad, no me presento para poner o quitar presidentes españoles.

P. ¿Qué pedirá Junts a cambio de facilitar la investidura? ¿Un referéndum? ¿Una nueva financiación?

R. Yo no estoy aquí para investir presidentes españoles y no me presento para ser presidenta de España. Me presento para poner Cataluña en el centro.

P. ¿Cree que se entiende que decidan vetar al candidato que ha propiciado la amnistía del expresidente de la Generalitat y presidente de Junts?

R. No ha propiciado nada, el señor Sánchez. Antes de las elecciones del 23 de julio de 2023, él mismo dijo que no a la amnistía. El propio president Illa dijo que ni amnistía ni nada. Es Junts quien ha arrastrado al Partido Socialista; le hemos forzado. Y, para mantener el poder, el Partido Socialista ha hecho todo lo que hemos pedido. Éramos conscientes de que el PSOE no lo hacía por voluntad propia, que lo hacía porque quería los votos, y nosotros hemos aprovechado esa fuerza. Por eso estoy convencida de que, si depende de Junts, tendremos el control de la inmigración, el control de nuestro dinero y podremos proteger nuestra lengua y nuestra nación.

P. ¿Está de acuerdo con quien dice que parte del desgaste que ha sufrido el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez es por haber facilitado la amnistía?

R. Si poner la agenda catalana en el centro desgasta a los partidos españoles, el problema lo tienen ellos. Ni le cuento todo el desgaste y toda la potencia mediática que hemos sufrido nosotros y no voy llorando por las esquinas.

P. ¿Teme que Junts sea visto como el partido que defiende a los propietarios y no tanto a la gente que tiene necesidad de acceder a una vivienda?

R. Luchar contra la propaganda que hay detrás de los dos grandes partidos españoles es complicado, pero estamos convencidos de lo que hemos hecho. Sobre vivienda, recomiendo leer el real decreto que ha aprobado el Consejo de Ministros, porque protege a los fondos buitre, a diferencia de lo que proponía Junts. También proponíamos que, para el inquilino que no puede pagar el alquiler, por el motivo que sea, automáticamente sea el Estado quien cubra la deuda y busque alternativa habitacional. Porque creemos que el pequeño propietario, ya tenga un piso, dos o tres, no tiene por qué asumir el gasto social. El peso de la vulnerabilidad tiene que asumirlo el Estado.

articles.preview: Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US. articles.body:
The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

Global pivots towards Asia

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.

The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.

China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.

Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
articles.summary: It is the latest development in a months-long challenge to the US president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links.
articles.preview: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations. Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.
articles.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline".

"The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

Her order will last until 28 November.

The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.

The historic course, which sits two miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service (NPS) in the nation's capital.

The legal fight then escalated in October when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.

After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate for the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post on Truth Social.

Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether justice department attorneys had "made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".

That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans had been "done in bad faith", and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.

She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

articles.body:
The failed federal Liberal candidate Katherine Deves, who campaigned to exclude transgender women from women’s sport, will stand for One Nation at next year’s New South Wales election.

Deves was among four NSW Legislative Council candidates announced by One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, on Sunday.

The other candidates were Arnon Wither, a construction worker from the Hunter region who works as an electorate officer for Senator Sean Bell; Manti Steele, a farmer, teacher and mother of eight from Dubbo; and Daniel Hill, a surf lifesaver from the state’s south coast.

The NSW election will be held on 13 March.

Newman said on Sunday the upper house candidates were “authentic”, “people from the real world” and not “career politicians”.

One Nation has only announced a single lower house candidate – Newman, in the electorate of Cessnock – but he said the party would run candidates in all 93 lower house seats.

“We want to make sure that these people bleed orange, and like I said, they’re all from the real world,” he said.

“That’s the that’s the type of person we’re aiming at … people from the real world who understand business, who understand their pinch points and pain points, understand the cost of living, understand cashflow.”

Deves was handpicked by the former prime minister Scott Morrison to run in the federal NSW seat of Warringah in 2022. Her candidacy was marred by controversy, including when she likened anti-trans activism to standing up against the Holocaust.

On Sunday she said she joined One Nation “because I wanted to be a part of the rescue, recovery, and restoration of our nation”.

“We are seeing cost of living skyrocket, whether it’s fuel, housing, energy, and we are watching a government that is so wedded to destructive ideologies like DEI and net zero that they are prepared to impoverish us all,” she said.

If elected, she would look to make changes to state laws regarding “discrimination, hate speech, vilification, birth certificates, etc”.

“Where we can restore clear and accurate language around biological sex, men and women, and ensure that women and girls are safe and have spaces for services, sports, etc, where it’s inappropriate for males to be there.”

One Nation has required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media.

News24 reported last month that Deves would run as an upper house candidate in the NSW election. She announced that she joined One Nation in September.

When Guardian Australia contacted Deves about her potential candidacy in October, she directed inquiries to Vikki Campion, the NSW party’s part-time media adviser. The party provided a statement saying it had confirmed only three candidates at that time – Newman, the lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, and a Tamworth firearms manufacturer, Jeff Bacon.

articles.title: UK government to consider changing age of consent after allegations against Russell Brand
articles.summary: Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’ The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl. articles.body:
The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl.

Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, she called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the newspaper that Latter’s “heart-breaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.

She said: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.

“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”

Under UK law, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.

Latter said: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about him, it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.

“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

Latter was referred to under the pseudonym of Alice in previous

She was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip.

He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.

She told the newspaper that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had confessed her age to him.

Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship.

Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.

She spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sex offence allegations against comedian David Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”.

Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’s accusers was asked to sign a non disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should also look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.

“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”

It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.

Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.

“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”

Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She added that it is “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”

Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing.

A Met Police spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

articles.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments - a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed".
articles.preview: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties". Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.
articles.body:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.

The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.

It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.

Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.

So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.

He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.

It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.

The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.

He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".

He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

articles.title: World leaders are coming to Shenzhen. What is China’s APEC message?
articles.summary: Analysts say the city’s transformation into a global tech hub makes it a fitting stage for next week’s APEC summit - showcasing China’s economic ambitions and push for deeper regional cooperation.
articles.preview: Analysts say the city’s transformation into a global tech hub makes it a fitting stage for next week’s APEC summit - showcasing China’s economic ambitions and push for deeper regional cooperation. SHENZHEN: Once a little-known border town comprising fishing villages and rural settlements on China’s southern coast, Shenzhen is now preparing to take centre stage as host of one of the year’s most closely watched diplomatic gatherings.
articles.body:
Analysts say the city’s transformation into a global tech hub makes it a fitting stage for next week’s APEC summit - showcasing China’s economic ambitions and push for deeper regional cooperation.

SHENZHEN: Once a little-known border town comprising fishing villages and rural settlements on China’s southern coast, Shenzhen is now preparing to take centre stage as host of one of the year’s most closely watched diplomatic gatherings.

As leaders from the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies prepare to gather in the Chinese megacity next week, Beijing hopes to showcase Shenzhen as a symbol of China's economic transformation - and a model of what it can now offer the region, analysts told CNA.

China has made openness, innovation and cooperation the priorities of its APEC host year, which will culminate in the Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Nov 18 and 19.

Analysts said Shenzhen’s evolution, from a magnet for foreign investment into a global technology powerhouse, makes it a fitting stage for that message.

For businesses, the test will be whether this year’s APEC summit produces practical measures that companies can actually adhere to and use, said Han Yonghui, a professor at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies (GDUFS).

“What matters more is which entities the measures apply to, when they take effect, whether transaction costs are reduced, and what channels of redress are available when disputes arise,” Han added.

FROM FACTORY FLOOR TO TECH POWERHOUSE: SHENZHEN’S RISE

With a population of more than 18 million, Shenzhen is now home to tech giants Huawei, Tencent, drone maker DJI and electric vehicle manufacturer BYD.

The city’s stunning rise from manufacturing base to global tech hub is central to why it was chosen to host this year’s APEC summit, said Xu Liping, an Asia-Pacific affairs expert at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).

“Shenzhen has progressed from a policy-based special zone to a model of institutional opening up, and made an industrial leap from the world's factory to an innovation engine,” Xu said.

Its transformation began in 1980, when it was designated one of China's first special economic zones - becoming a testing ground for market-oriented policies aimed at attracting foreign investment, technology and management expertise.

Late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping’s landmark southern tour in 1992, which included a stop in Shenzhen, gave fresh momentum to China’s economic reforms.

Under President Xi Jinping, ambitions widened beyond the city. Shenzhen is now one of four core engines of the Greater Bay Area - a grand initiative to connect Hong Kong, Macau and nine Guangdong cities more closely through finance, research, manufacturing and trade.

Han from GDUFS said the city’s role had evolved and taken on more importance - from bringing in foreign capital and expertise to helping Chinese companies develop technology and expand into overseas markets.

“China’s deepening opening up is reflected in its greater capacity to jointly organise research and development, production and services with external partners while continuing to absorb global resources,” Han said.

Shenzhen-based cybersecurity and cloud computing firm Sangfor Technologies is just one example.

Founded in 2000, it began expanding overseas in 2008 and now serves more than 100,000 customers in over 100 countries and regions, according to the company.

Keith Lee, Sangfor's cloud business director, said the challenge had shifted from convincing overseas customers of its products and value to better understanding their needs.

"The challenge is no longer about proving the value of technology made in Shenzhen. It is about understanding what each customer needs as the landscape continues to evolve," Lee said.

When Window of the World, a local Shenzhen theme park, first opened in 1994, its miniature replicas of global landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Mount Rushmore drew crowds of curious visitors - eager for a glimpse of places they might never see in person.

Decades on, the landmarks remain but the park has evolved. Robots, digital services and drone displays from Shenzhen companies now feature prominently.

Employee Wang Chao, a 44-year-old marketing executive from Hubei who joined the park in 2006, has witnessed that transformation firsthand.

“In the past, it was inconvenient for Chinese people to travel abroad, so they could come to Window of the World and see things from other countries,” Wang told CNA.

"Now, when foreign visitors come, they can also see things from Shenzhen and China through Window of the World," he said.

CHINA’S APEC JOURNEY

China has hosted APEC twice before - with this year’s summit in Shenzhen marking its third turn as host.

The first was in Shanghai in 2001, when China was also preparing to join the World Trade Organization. The central question then, said Xu from CASS, was how the country would integrate into the global economy.

By the time Beijing hosted the summit in 2014, China was the world’s second-largest economy and seeking a greater role in shaping regional cooperation.

That summit produced a roadmap towards a proposed Asia-Pacific free trade area and a plan to improve connectivity.

“This marked China’s shift from participant to agenda-setter,” Xu said.

This year's Shenzhen summit marks another shift, he added - from how China joins the global economy to what it believes it can contribute to the region.

OPEN FOR BUSINESS?

But how far does Shenzhen’s reputation for openness translate into real opportunities for foreign firms and businesses?

Singaporean entrepreneur Juana Lee, also the founder and CEO of Far Vision Consultancy, has experienced first hand both opportunities and challenges of operating in the city.

Lee first came to China in 2002 - helping relatives manage factories that produced scarves, sunglasses and umbrellas.

Work took her to the Longgang district, where she recalled ageing factories, pollution, poor transportation links and difficulty finding reliable information in English.

“It was a manufacturing world (then),” she said.

After leaving the family business around 2013, Lee set up a consultancy helping foreign companies navigate the Chinese market.

Shenzhen’s relatively low operating costs, compared with cities like Hong Kong and Singapore, made it easier for entrepreneurs to recover from financial setbacks while starting businesses, Lee said.

The city’s close proximity to Hong Kong was another draw. A direct high-speed train ride from Futian station to Hong Kong’s West Kowloon takes around 15 minutes.

But Lee has also seen newcomers struggle with unrealistic expectations - failing to understand local rules and encountering difficulties obtaining reliable information.

Some underestimate the responsibilities of running a company in the city, she said.

The businesses that do last are the ones led by owners willing to persist and learn from setbacks, she said.

Despite Shenzhen’s reputation for openness, foreign companies still encounter various barriers such as local protectionism, preferences for domestic firms and requirements to buy Chinese products, said Allan von Mehren, chief China analyst at Danske Bank.

“You can argue that Shenzhen as a symbol of openness often contrasts with the reality many foreign businesses meet when they enter the Chinese market,” he added.

THE SHENZHEN ADVANTAGE

Yet for foreign businesses to navigate and overcome those barriers, Shenzhen offers an advantage over other Chinese cities - the ability to develop ideas quickly and turn them into products.

When Singaporean entrepreneur Amit Kumar arrived at Shenzhen's Chaihuo Makerspace in June, he brought two bare circuit boards and a 3D-printed casing, according to its general manager, Ye Yu.

Kumar, founder of Singapore-based robotics and edtech firm Farm2Future Innovations, was developing an AI-powered tutor designed to answer school questions in multiple Indian languages.

Despite having no previous soldering experience, Kumar managed to assemble two working prototypes, Ye said - also developing firmware for an animated interface and launching a pre-order page within 48 hours.

He planned to return to Shenzhen to develop production moulds, build a supply chain and finalise the product, Ye added.

When Ye joined Chaihuo in 2013, its members were mainly enthusiasts experimenting with open-source hardware and robots.

Today, the community has expanded - now attracting people working in sectors like agriculture, education and environmental work - who want to turn their ideas into physical products.

Developers are able to draw on Shenzhen’s vast network, she said. They can source materials like chips, circuit boards, as well as casings and moulds - and also find factories able to produce small test batches while adjusting them as designs evolve.

“What makes Shenzhen special is that it greatly shortens the distance between an idea and a product,” Ye said.

BEYOND APEC

Speaking at a briefing on Saturday (Nov 14), Shenzhen Mayor Li Yun said measures introduced to make the city more convenient for overseas visitors - covering entry, transport, payments, education and healthcare - would be made permanent if they proved effective.

“We will do everything possible to turn the outcomes of hosting APEC into development gains that better benefit all residents,” he said.

Whether APEC can turn Shenzhen’s economic strengths into broader regional cooperation - while also easing concerns over market access and competition - remains to be seen, analysts said.

Analysts said much would depend on what APEC economies agree in Shenzhen, as US-China competition continues to reshape trade, technology and global supply chains.

This week, China extended its trade truce with the US ahead of the APEC summit, where Trump is expected to meet Xi.

But wider disputes over tech and market access remain unresolved.

“China needs to respond to external uncertainty with the certainty of cooperation,” said Han from GDUFS.

Xu from CASS noted that Singapore and other Southeast Asian economies could benefit from closer links in digital payments, services trade and green development - but would also be concerned about access to China’s market, dependence on Chinese suppliers and competition from larger Chinese companies.

Businesses would want clearer rules on fair competition and cross-border data flows, said Han - and would also want to know how investment could improve local skills and industrial capacity.

“What the Shenzhen summit promises is to translate cooperative consensus into institutional arrangements that enterprises can actually use,” he added.

Paperless trade offers one practical test.

If customs and other trade systems across APEC economies can recognise the same electronic documents, companies could spend less time submitting paperwork repeatedly when moving goods across borders.

APEC research estimates that paperless trade could cut transaction costs by almost 6 per cent.

Han said progress could include connecting electronic documents directly with customs systems, alongside clearer rules covering cross-border data, AI and product standards.

The two-day APEC CEO Summit, which will begin on Nov 17, is expected to produce a “Shenzhen Initiative” - outlining commitments from the regional business community.

Organisers have announced broad priorities including openness, inclusion, innovation and connectivity - but have yet to release detailed measures.

For businesses, observers say the value of any pledge will depend on when it takes effect - which companies can use it and whether it reduces the cost and uncertainty of operating across borders.

articles.title: Jordan sentences three men to death by hanging after deadly church attack
articles.summary: This is a breaking news story.
articles.preview: Three men have been convicted of carrying out an attack on a church in the Karak governorate that killed nine people. A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south. Gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan’s Karak governorate on October 23.
articles.body:
Three men have been convicted of carrying out an attack on a church in the Karak governorate that killed nine people.

A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south.

Gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan’s Karak governorate on October 23.

Authorities said three men, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, had fled after the attack and were arrested three days later.

In a statement on Sunday, the Jordanian military said the “State Security Court issued its ruling sentencing to death the three criminals who carried out the terrorist attack” at the church.

Crimes listed

The court found them guilty of “committing terrorist attacks” resulting in death, as well as weapons offences, “conspiracy to commit terrorist acts” and “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation”.

“One of the perpetrators of the terrorist operation was also convicted of providing funds with the intention of using them to finance the commission of terrorist acts,” it added.

In late October, Jordanian security forces arrested the three men suspected of the attack that targeted the St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Karak, after clashing with them.

The governorate is home to many members of Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s 11.5 million people.

King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties” as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to attacks after the incident.

articles.title: ASEAN summit: Who’s attending and what’s at stake?
articles.summary: Energy disruptions as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran is a key issue for the import-dependent bloc.
