articles.body:
Energy disruptions as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran is a key issue for the import-dependent bloc.

Southeast Asian countries that comprise the ASEAN economic bloc will meet in the Philippines this week as the region continues to bear the brunt of oil shortages caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as by US-China rivalry, which has hit economies hard.

The Manila summit will be held from November 15 to 17 and will include US President Donald Trump and several other world leaders.

The 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) aims to establish a single market, although it cannot impose decisions on members. It comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and East Timor, with a combined population of nearly 694 million, or 8.4 percent of the world’s population.

Several ASEAN meetings are held annually. This week’s summit is expected to be the final one for this year.

Beyond the energy crisis, other pressing issues include disputes over the South China Sea and trade.

Here’s what we know:

Who is attending?

In addition to leaders and representatives from the 11 member countries, other guests include:

- US President Donald Trump – Trump is expected to hold a special summit with ASEAN members on November 17 as Washington’s trade tensions with China continue. He is also set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Afterwards, Trump is due to head to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting on 18-19 November.

- India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi – Although India is not part of ASEAN, India is a key trading partner to member states.

- Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney – Carney is set to give a speech at the summit.

- Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva – His visit will be the first by a sitting Brazilian president to the Philippines. He is expected to discuss trade, defence and other areas of cooperation with ASEAN members.

- Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov – His visit comes after the Russia-ASEAN summit in July.

What are the key issues?

US-Iran war

The summit is being held at a time when Southeast Asian countries have been hit hard by shortages in oil and gas supplies from Middle Eastern suppliers amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia are among the most vulnerable to the energy disruptions in the Gulf, with Manila declaring a state of national energy emergency in March.

Millions of ASEAN citizens also live and work in the Middle East, where the war threatens their safety and earnings.

Meanwhile, Asian countries are worried the conflict could spill into the Strait of Malacca, a narrow waterway between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

Trade

The US’s tariff war has seen ASEAN countries slapped with 10-12.5 percent tariff hikes since the beginning of US President Donald Trump’s second term in the White House, prompting the bloc to strengthen trade relationships elsewhere.

South China Sea

China and four ASEAN members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – as well as Taiwan, have been locked in decades of territorial standoffs in the busy waterway.

The area is important as it is believed to host undersea deposits of oil and gas.

In 2005, the bloc began negotiating a “code of conduct” with China to discourage aggression and prevent major clashes. The negotiations have often stalled, however, partly due to flared tensions, especially between Manila and Beijing in recent years.

In 2023, the two sides agreed to speed things up and release a finished draft this year. At least 10 rounds of talks have been held this year, led by Malaysia, with a final round taking place in October.

However, analysts doubt a definite conclusion will be reached at the summit this week, meaning talks could continue into next year.

Thailand-Cambodia tensions

Armed clashes broke out between the two ASEAN member states late last year along an 800km (500-mile) contested border area, as well as over competing claims to sacred religious sites, such as the Preah Vihear Shiva temple.

At least 150 people were reported to have been killed, and nearly one million displaced.

ASEAN members, as well as China and the US, intervened, leading to talks. Although a ceasefire has been in place since December, the wider border dispute remains unresolved, and the bloc is calling for more dialogue and the participation of third-party observers.

Myanmar conflict

The ongoing civil war in Myanmar, which has compounded the Rohingya refugee crisis, has been at the top of the agenda as the bloc pushes for the restoration of democracy in the country.

Multiple rebel forces, some of them ethnic-based armed groups, have been fighting the military government since the country’s February 2021 coup.

ASEAN has already restricted Myanmar’s participation at important summits to non-political representatives as concerns about violence and a humanitarian crisis grow.

The bloc’s five-point Myanmar peace plan, launched in April 2021 and calling for dialogue and improved humanitarian aid access, has meanwhile failed to alleviate the situation.

Cross-border haze

Months of widespread wildfires in drought-hit Indonesia have scorched an estimated 2.88 million hectares (7.12 million acres) and resulted in at least 3,500 deaths.

The resulting haze has severely impacted not just the country’s residents, but also those in neighbouring Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and East Timor.

Jakarta has faced criticism for failing to effectively respond to the fires, but the government has defended its approach, saying thousands of responders have been deployed.

articles.body:
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. Likened to the 1945 summit at Yalta, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

Zelensky has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”, invoking the conference in Crimea when the then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary: International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes. The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war. Continue reading...
articles.body:
The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.

The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.

Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.

“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.

A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.

Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.

“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.

During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.

The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.

This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

The former general is separately being investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.

More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.

A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.

“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

articles.title: Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
articles.summary: Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter. Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel. But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity. He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war. "I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday. Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming. CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way. Trump told bin Salman on 31 October that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion. Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Trump has spoken with Erdogan three times since 28 October, according to Turkey's presidency. An official readout from the 7 November call stressed that tensions between Iran and the US need to end. MILITARY OPTIONS At the same time, the US military is ready to escalate if needed, three more people familiar with US planning said. A third aircraft carrier is moving into the Middle East in the coming days to replace one of the two currently operating in the region, but all three carriers could stay if needed, the people said. Trump could opt to bomb Iran's underground nuclear facilities, one of the people familiar with Trump's calls with the Saudi and Turkish leaders said. But the US has already struck those facilities, and it is unclear whether further strikes would be successful. ISRAELI PRESSURE Israeli officials have continued to lobby the administration to engage in another military campaign, according to a US official. Trump signalled this week that the US has already achieved what it could from negotiations, but did not say whether he would resume strikes. articles.title: Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
articles.summary: Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah.
articles.preview: Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah, a pro-Iranian armed group. Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group. Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
articles.body:
Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah, a pro-Iranian armed group.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group.

Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities.

“In light of the investigation’s findings, [the prime minister] ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said.

The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said.

The police chief of Babil province was among those dismissed.

Iran-aligned armed group

Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption.

Senior Iraqi politicians previously told the AFP news agency that al-Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to confront groups refusing to disarm.

Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, said previous Iraqi governments had been careful not to address the issue of an alleged oil smuggling network worth up to $30m monthly.

“This area had effectively been run as a state within a state until now,” Smith said. “But that seems to have changed, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi saying that no inch of Iraq will be allowed to have oil smuggling operations like this.”

Two strategic oil pipelines running through the south of the country, just south of Baghdad, “had effectively been tapped into”, Smith said, citing a leaked intelligence report. “Oil was being siphoned off, stolen, and then sold on the black market in an operation worth tens of millions of dollars every month.”

On Wednesday, the INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf al-Nasr, accusing an unnamed group of tapping into a pipeline there.

Al-Numan said the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.

Akeel Abbas, a senior non-resident fellow at the Iraq Initiative within the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera that oil smuggling by various political factions and armed groups “is common in Iraq” due to “commercial rather than political or strategic” gains.

Abbas said the latest crackdown has more to do with “militia disarmament”.

“The prime minister cleverly decided to frame it as anticorruption. That is why a few days ago, there was a report leaked by the government about this operation,” he said.

The prime minister wants to “cut off the financial lifeline to this particular group that has been so resistant” to the government’s “militia disarmament” initiatives, he added.

articles.title: Sudan: Misery worsens amid plummeting aid for displaced people
articles.summary: Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.
articles.preview: November 14, 2026 Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan.
articles.body:
November 14, 2026

Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan. Without urgent provision of flexible funding, even more families will have to cope without adequate protection from extreme weather conditions, insecurity, violence and exploitation in the coming months.

According to a recently published joint statement, $2.9 billion (€2.62bn) is needed for the United Nation's Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. This funding is intended to provide life-saving aid to 20.4 million people in Sudan. So far, however, only 47% of the required funds have been raised.

A total of 33.7 million people in the war- and famine-stricken country are dependent on humanitarian aid. Some 15.4 million alone require emergency shelter and basic household items. However, due to a lack of funding, aid organizations have been able to assist only 10%.

More than three and a half years after the war began between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is still the site of the world's largest humanitarian and displacement crisis. About 8.6 million people fled within the country to escape the escalating violence and more than 4.6 million fled to neighboring countries. Another 5.2 million have returned to their regions of origin despite the ongoing war. However, their towns and infrastructure have been destroyed. Fighting, drone strikes and logistical problems further complicate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

Between 40,000 and 250,000 people have been killed. Accurate or updated figures are not available as fighting continues, satellite-based internet communication is curbed, and many aid organizations and observers have left the country.

Donors cut back on funding

"It's hard to imagine how people are supposed to survive," Marina Peter, chairwoman of the Sudan and South Sudan Forum in Germany, told DW. In large parts of the country, people have been cut off from humanitarian aid since the war began. Some have survived by eating roots. According to the Sudan expert, the fact that people are still returning to war zones from neighboring countries is also linked to shortages: Food rations have been drastically cut in refugee camps.

Ivo Körner, Sudan specialist at Caritas International, criticizes the international community for the sharp decline in aid. "Globally, we're seeing a dramatic drop in funding for humanitarian aid," Körner told DW. It's not just the United States that has slashed its contributions; Germany and the European Union are also providing significantly less funding than they did four or five years ago, he said.

In Sudan, Caritas International supports refugees and the communities hosting them with cash assistance, drinking water supplies, basic medical care and seeds. However, Sudan's Caritas' projects in 2026 have been financed exclusively through donations. While Körner hopes for additional funding from the German Foreign Office for Sudan projects, he predicts that funding opportunities will be significantly more limited than in previous years.

According to Sudan expert Marina Peters, the consequences of the crisis are becoming increasingly difficult to assess. "In many parts of the country, people have already been completely cut off from humanitarian aid since the start of the war," she told DW. Peter also notes that child mortality in Sudan is above average. However, it is nearly impossible to determine the actual extent of the crisis more precisely because the warring parties continue to obstruct humanitarian access.

Who should take action?

On October 23, the United Kingdom and 31 other international partners, including Germany, issued a joint statement on the looming famine in Sudan. According to the statement, 19.5 million people — about 41% of the population — are suffering from acute food insecurity. The countries are calling on the warring parties to allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure. At the same time, they are demanding an increase in international aid funding.

While Marina Peter welcomes the appeal in principle, she sees a contradiction. "The question is: Who is this appeal actually directed at?" Most of the signatories have themselves systematically cut funding for humanitarian aid and development cooperation. The appeal to the international donor community is thus ultimately directed at the states themselves.

Meanwhile, the Sudanese government based in the country's capital Khartoum — led by General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan's SAF — rejects all warnings of a famine.

In a statement dated October 26, it claims that the food situation in the country is reportedly reassuring and that government reserves and ongoing agricultural production are sufficient to meet demand. According to Khartoum, the warnings from Western countries amount to a politicization of the humanitarian situation.

Peter criticized this statement as "truly cynical and almost perfidious. The government's claim that humanitarian organizations have unrestricted access also does not reflect reality, she said. In many places, aid continues to be obstructed.

Drone attacks exacerbate dangers

In addition to hunger and displacement, the threat to civilians posed by the use of drones is also growing. The Peace for Sudan Platform issued an appeal on November 5 calling for an end to attacks on civilians, markets, hospitals, and water and electricity supplies. In the first three weeks of October alone, at least 306 people were killed in attacks. According to the UN Human Rights Office, drones claimed the lives of at least 1,120 civilians in the first half of 2026.

"Drone strikes are a major problem," Caritas' Körner confirmed. They cause widespread anxiety among the population and often strike civilians. Added to this is the danger to humanitarian workers. This makes local partner organizations all the more important, he said. They enjoy the trust of the local population, are deeply rooted in the regions and in some cases are able to reach areas that international aid workers can hardly access.

This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China: White House
articles.summary: US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting.
articles.preview: US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting. WASHINGTON: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first-ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday (Nov 13).
articles.body:
US officials say President Donald Trump plans to discuss nuclear arms reductions and the war in Iran with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, in what would be an unprecedented trilateral meeting.

WASHINGTON: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first-ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday (Nov 13).

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran - but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.

The Kremlin said later on Saturday that the trilateral meet will take place on Nov 19.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.

YALTA REDUX?

The meeting calls back to the 1945 Yalta summit in the Soviet Union, where then-US president Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.

Zelenskyy has raised the alarm that the meeting in Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like "redistribution of spheres of influence" for the 21st century.

The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the "Western hemisphere" - including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January - but splitting the world among great powers like it's 1945 may not guarantee security.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president's return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump's meetings with Xi, the officials said.

"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.

Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.

articles.title: DR Congo: Bukavu comedy festival offers laughter amid the ongoing conflict
articles.summary: For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and the DRC offer residents a moment of relaxation and hope.
articles.preview: Democratic Republic Of Congo The ninth edition of the International Zero Polémique Festival takes place from 9 to 15 November in Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire and the DRC take to the stage to celebrate comedy and offer residents a moment of escape in a region deeply affected by armed violence. Bursts of laughter temporarily overshadowed the anxieties of everyday life as spectators gather to watch performances at the Bukavu Comedy Club.
articles.body:
Democratic Republic Of Congo

The ninth edition of the International Zero Polémique Festival takes place from 9 to 15 November in Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

For one week, comedians from the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire and the DRC take to the stage to celebrate comedy and offer residents a moment of escape in a region deeply affected by armed violence.

Bursts of laughter temporarily overshadowed the anxieties of everyday life as spectators gather to watch performances at the Bukavu Comedy Club.

On stage, comedians take turns sharing anecdotes, improvisations, and jokes. Laughter echoes across the room as applause fills the venue.

The festive atmosphere contrasts sharply with the difficulties faced by the population in recent months. For local performers, the enthusiastic response from the audience is a genuine source of satisfaction.

Beyond the artistic performance itself, making people laugh in an environment marked by stress and uncertainty takes on particular significance.

“It is a pleasure to see so many people laughing at your jokes when we are going through stressful and difficult times. Being able to make people laugh really makes me happy,” says Jospin De Mars, a comedian based in Bukavu.

The festival also provides an opportunity to strengthen exchanges between artists of different nationalities as they share their experiences and artistic styles.

For Jojo La Légende, a comedian from the Republic of Congo, the audience's warm response to his performances are among the most memorable aspects of the festival.

“It brings me joy. I am moved to see that these are people who need happiness, people who need laughter. They are happy, they are delighted,” he says.

“Where there are smiles, there is joy, peace, good health and a positive atmosphere,” he adds.

People in the eastern DRC have lived for several decades amid armed conflicts, forced displacement, and successive humanitarian crises.

In Bukavu, which remains under the control of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), uncertainty persists as clashes continue in several surrounding areas.

In this context, cultural and artistic activities take on a significance that goes beyond simple entertainment.

They provide spaces for people to meet, offer a temporary break from isolation and help maintain a sense of social life despite ongoing tensions.

For some spectators, attending these performances is also a way to regain a sense of lightness and a way to recharge.

Joseph Haadi, a resident of Bukavu, explains that these moments allow him to learn, meet new people, and better manage stress.

“Honestly, it sometimes helps me grow and gain knowledge. It also makes us happy when we are stressed, then we come here,” he says.

While humour cannot erase the trauma of war or resolve the difficulties facing residents, it offers a form of collective relief.

For the duration of a performance, everyday worries fade into the background, making room for sharing, smiles, and togetherness.

Beyond the shows, the festival also aims to promote cultural exchanges and encourage encounters between artists from different backgrounds.

By bringing together comedians from several African countries, the event turns laughter into a common language capable of transcending borders and differences.

This international dimension helps position Bukavu within a broader regional cultural landscape, despite its particularly challenging security environment.

Over seven days of performances and encounters, it serves as a reminder that culture retains its importance, even during the most difficult times.

While laughter does not make the war disappear, in a city where the future remains unclear, these shared smiles carry a particular meaning.

They reflect a population that, despite its hardships, continues to find reasons to come together and hold on to hope.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv hospital, leave two dead in Odesa
articles.summary: Russian overnight attacks on Ukraine killed at least two person in Odesa and injured another at a hospital in Kyiv. Rescuers evacuated patients, including people using wheelchairs and crutches, as firefighters battled the flames.
articles.preview: In the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district, a strike sparked a fire at a medical facility and partially destroyed its second floor, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. articles.body: In the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district, a strike sparked a fire at a medical facility and partially destroyed its second floor, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. Hospital staff evacuated 30 people, while emergency crews rescued another seven. Footage released by the emergency service shows patients being helped to safety, including people using wheelchairs and crutches, as firefighters work to extinguish the blaze. Other images reveal damaged windows, smoke rising from the building and rescue workers moving through hospital corridors. The fire had been extinguished. In the southern port city of Odesa, a separate Russian drone attack killed two people and injured five others, according to Serhii Lysak, head of the city's military administration. A private house and several vehicles were also damaged in the strikes, while nighttime footage shows firefighters tackling a blaze at the scene. The attacks affected two major Ukrainian cities, with emergency services responding to fires, damaged buildings and casualties. In Kyiv, the evacuation of patients highlighted the disruption caused when medical facilities are struck, particularly for people with reduced mobility. The incidents come as Russia continues its aerial attacks on Ukraine more than four years after launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Cairo Film Festival opens as Middle East war weighs on cinema
articles.summary: The 47th Cairo International Film Festival got underway on Wednesday in the Egyptian capital. The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world. This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war.
articles.preview: Egypt The 47th Cairo International Film Festival got underway on Wednesday in the Egyptian capital. The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world. This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war. Screenwriter, poet, and producer Medhat El-Adl was honoured with a Golden Pyramid for lifetime achievement.
articles.body:
Egypt

The 47th Cairo International Film Festival got underway on Wednesday in the Egyptian capital. The event brings together filmmakers, actors and other prominent figures from around the world.

This year’s festival is taking place under the shadow of the Middle East war.

Screenwriter, poet, and producer Medhat El-Adl was honoured with a Golden Pyramid for lifetime achievement.

He says the war affects whether audiences are able to see the films being produced:

"Of course, any war, conflict zone, or tension doesn't just affect cinema, it impacts people's livelihoods. Consequently, people will prioritise earning a living over going to the movie theater. So it has had a very strong impact on everything. If I have 10 cents, will I buy food or spend it on a movie ticket? I'll buy food! So it has affected us in one way or another, and that's just financially speaking.”

The financial situation is pushing production costs through the roof, with no guarantee the outlay will be recovered, says Egyptian actress Gehad Hossam:

"The war is affecting the entire region, the economics of the industry have been impacted because something you used to produce, per say, for 5 EGP suddenly costs 10 EGP, while the market can't absorb or cover that cost increase. It's a tough situation.”

For film critic Tarek El-Shinnawi, Egypt’s film industry faces other challenges - notably restrictions on free speech that limit what filmmakers are able to express:

"We just need the ceiling of censorship to be a bit higher, what Egypt lacks is a censor with a broader horizon, and to open the door for discussing all issues, a great film isn't the one with a high budget or a massive production cost - no, a great film is one that carries an idea and offers freedom to the creator.”

For festival president Hussein Fahmi, the event isn’t only about showcasing contemporary films but also preserving Egypt’s cultural heritage:

"Cinema is not simply entertainment but a record of human experience, social transformations, and historical moments, preserving stories and emotions for generations to come," Fahmi said in his opening remarks.

The festival runs until 20 November.

articles.title: Che cosa sta facendo l’Italia per difendersi dagli attacchi informatici
articles.summary: I numeri sono in aumento e negli ultimi anni sono state introdotte nuove regole e stanziate risorse per prevenire e contrastare le minacce. Ma capire quanto queste misure abbiano funzionato non è semplice
articles.preview: L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.
articles.body:
L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.

Questi episodi si inseriscono in un quadro che ha riportato l’attenzione sulle minacce informatiche e la capacità dell’Italia di contrastarle efficacemente. Il 7 novembre il ministero degli Esteri aveva reso nota la diffusione sul dark web di dati personali del ministro Antonio Tajani. Il Ministro ha collegato le minacce alla posizione italiana sulla guerra in Ucraina e ha chiesto di affrontare il tema delle minacce ibride al G7 degli Esteri, che si è svolto a Parigi il 9 e 10 novembre. Un altro episodio era stato registrato a inizio novembre, quando alcuni supermercati italiani erano stati colpiti da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione, sui cui il governo aveva fatto il punto in una riunione il 3 novembre.

Il 9 novembre il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto, in un’intervista al Corriere della Sera, ha definito la guerra ibrida una «sfida epocale», che deve essere affrontata tramite una strategia comune tra le istituzioni. Una posizione in linea con quanto detto qualche giorno dalla presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni, che aveva richiamato l’attenzione sui possibili effetti degli attacchi informatici, sottolineando i rischi per le infrastrutture civili.

Negli ultimi anni, l’Italia ha introdotto nuove regole, istituito strutture dedicate alla cybersicurezza e stanziato risorse per proteggere le proprie infrastrutture digitali. Ma quali interventi sono stati realizzati e che cosa dicono i dati disponibili sulla loro efficacia?

articles.title: Che cosa ha deciso la Corte costituzionale su Giusi Bartolozzi
articles.summary: È stato accolto solo in parte il conflitto di attribuzione sollevato dalla Camera, e ora l’ex capa di gabinetto di Nordio potrà essere processata per false dichiarazioni
articles.preview: Che cosa succede adesso La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali.
articles.body:
Che cosa succede adesso

La decisione ha conseguenze diverse per le due questioni esaminate. Per quanto riguarda l’eventuale concorso nei reati ministeriali, ora il Tribunale dei ministri dovrà esplicitare le ragioni per cui non lo ha configurato e la Procura dovrà comunicarle alla Camera. Quest’ultima potrà contestare la valutazione dei magistrati attraverso un nuovo conflitto di attribuzione, qualora ritenga che la mancata configurazione del concorso abbia indebitamente sottratto Bartolozzi alla procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. In quel caso, la Corte costituzionale dovrebbe verificare se la valutazione dei magistrati abbia leso le prerogative della Camera, non accertare la responsabilità penale di Bartolozzi.

Quanto alle presunte false informazioni, il procedimento prosegue secondo le regole ordinarie, senza necessità di autorizzazione parlamentare. La Procura ha già emesso un decreto di citazione diretta a giudizio nei confronti di Bartolozzi, che quindi potrà andare a processo.

Resta da chiarire se Bartolozzi avrebbe dovuto essere ascoltata come indagata, anziché come persona informata sui fatti. In quest’ultimo caso era tenuta a dire la verità, ed è proprio dalle dichiarazioni rese in questa veste che è nata l’accusa di false informazioni. Se fosse stata ascoltata come indagata, avrebbe invece avuto il diritto di non rispondere. La Corte costituzionale ha lasciato aperta la questione delle eventuali conseguenze sui suoi diritti di difesa. La procura prospetta, dal canto suo, un’altra eventualità: se nel corso del giudizio per false informazioni dovessero emergere indizi di concorso nei reati attribuiti a Nordio, il giudice dovrebbe assolvere Bartolozzi e restituire gli atti al pubblico ministero, per avviare la procedura prevista per i reati ministeriali. Anche su questo profilo la Corte non si è pronunciata.

articles.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
articles.summary: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.preview: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.body:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)

Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”

It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

articles.title: I bot si ribellano ai politici, 'colpa' di Microsoft down
articles.summary: Messaggi da account sospetti. Salvini: 'Ci insultano'. Non si parli di hacker russi
articles.preview: "Non posso scrivere un messaggio volto a insultare uno specifico partito politico" oppure "Non posso scrivere uno specifico messaggio finalizzato a convincere specifici eurodeputati a sostenere una proposta legislativa". Questi i messaggi comparsi nelle ultime ore e in modo massivo sulle pagine social di alcuni politici italiani, dal leader della Lega Matteo Salvini agli eurodeputati di FdI e Pd, Carlo Fidanza e Dario Nardella.
articles.body:
"Non posso scrivere un messaggio volto a insultare uno specifico partito politico" oppure "Non posso scrivere uno specifico messaggio finalizzato a convincere specifici eurodeputati a sostenere una proposta legislativa". Questi i messaggi comparsi nelle ultime ore e in modo massivo sulle pagine social di alcuni politici italiani, dal leader della Lega Matteo Salvini agli eurodeputati di FdI e Pd, Carlo Fidanza e Dario Nardella. La "rivolta dei bot contro i politici", la chiama Repubblica.it che mette in relazione i commenti seriali proveniente da "account sospetti" con il recente malfunzionamento di Microsoft e dei software di intelligenza artificiale (OpenAI e Anthropic).

La reazione della politica non si fa attendere, con il vicepremier Matteo Salvini che punta il dito: "Profili falsi arrivavano sui profili della Lega ad insultare e sulle pagine del Pd a glorificare. Vediamo chi c'è dietro. Voglio che siano le forze dell'ordine a capire. Spero che nessuno in questo caso tiri fuori gli hacker russi...". Ancor più duro il senatore Claudio Borghi secondo cui "è bastato un malfunzionamento per scoprire che, invece degli hacker russi, ci sono italianissimi personaggi ad inquinare il dibattito politico con schiere di bot addestrati per attaccare, guarda caso, la Lega e Matteo Salvini. In realtà la cosa non ci stupisce particolarmente: da tempo erano emerse notizie di squadre informatiche addestrate da PD, M5S e persino dalla UE per coordinare gli attacchi contro gli avversari politici". Ma anche Avs chiede chiarezza.

Angelo Bonelli riferisce di essere stato lui per primo vittima di questo fenomeno: "I miei profili sono costantemente assaliti da commenti minacciosi e insultanti". Di qui l'auspicio di un inchiesta della magistratura sulle "reti di account automatizzati che usano l'intelligenza artificiale per condizionare il dibattito politico". Sono domande che riguardano la tenuta della nostra democrazia". Si unisce all'appello Elisabetta Piccolotti: "Non accettiamo che anche la prossima campagna elettorale si svolga in un mare di immondizia", servono "norme tese ad assicurare una par condicio digitale per le prossime elezioni: le piattaforme vanno obbligate a cancellare o sterilizzare i bot, i contenuti prodotti con l'intelligenza artificiale vanno resi chiaramente identificabili, le operazioni dall'estero vanno fermate e il regolamento europeo sulla pubblicità politica deve essere attuato individuando l'agenzia deputata ai controlli e alle sanzioni".

articles.preview: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.
articles.body:
A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

articles.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

articles.body:
November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.preview: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago. Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
articles.body:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

OpenAI has taken several stumbles

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

Apple’s Siri AI

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs. This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Character.ai

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Microsoft’s Recall

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22.

Humane AI Pin

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

Rabbit R1

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down.
