articles.preview: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. CSET’s Helen Toner says ‘we’re screwed’ if our AI safety plan rests on any one person being trusted to get this right. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.” With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day. I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning? They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for. In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?” We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions. [Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight. They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology. The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.” Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with. It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined. There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate? A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey. I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do. There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events. You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well. This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means. It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well. Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?” The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. DeepMind, when it was founded in 2010, was an AGI company and at the time it was like, “Wow, what a bunch of weirdos.” The same thing was true of OpenAI when it was founded at the end of 2015. They were an AGI company and that was a very weird thing to say and a very weird thing to be. What we’ve seen over the past 10 years is that bunch of weirdos who had this weird belief that the AI systems we can build are not just great B2B SaaS products. They’re not just fun chatbots. They’re going to fundamentally change the nature of the universe. That group of people keeps being right in the sense of building the best AI systems that the most people want to use and that make the most money. I think you have that set of true believers — which is very concentrated in OpenAI and Anthropic, but there are also some of them at Google, Meta, and SpaceX — and they haven’t been right about everything, to be clear, but their star has risen. So you now have people who are not AGI-pilled feeling like they have to pander to those who are so that they can attract the good researchers who will build their good B2B SaaS products. But if you’re just saying AGI-pilled things so that you can hire the researchers to build the B2B SaaS, then you’re not actually going to get there.

articles.body:
Microsoft

Multinational technology corporation, Microsoft, has apologised for a global service outage that left millions of users unable to use its apps for more than 24 hours.

It said on Saturday that service has been restored across Teams, Outlook, and its other products, ending the shutdown that crippled online communications for businesses, governments, and individual users.

Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.

The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars, and hosting virtual meetings.

Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.

The outage was one of the longest in software giant’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.

The incident highlighted concerns about the world’s reliance on the company’s workplace software.

articles.title: Un problema per Nvidia è un problema per l’AI
articles.summary: Dalla società che era guidata da Jensen Huang dipende buona parte del settore: ora ci possono essere sia crisi sia opportunità
articles.preview: Dalla società che era guidata da Jensen Huang dipende buona parte del settore: ora ci possono essere sia crisi sia opportunità Le dimissioni di Jensen Huang da CEO di Nvidia non riguardano solamente la società che aveva contribuito a fondare, una delle più ricche del mondo, ma anche l’intero settore dell’intelligenza artificiale (AI). I processori Nvidia sono centrali per il funzionamento e lo sviluppo dei nuovi modelli di AI, in particolare di quelli più avanzati.
articles.body:
Dalla società che era guidata da Jensen Huang dipende buona parte del settore: ora ci possono essere sia crisi sia opportunità

Le dimissioni di Jensen Huang da CEO di Nvidia non riguardano solamente la società che aveva contribuito a fondare, una delle più ricche del mondo, ma anche l’intero settore dell’intelligenza artificiale (AI). I processori Nvidia sono centrali per il funzionamento e lo sviluppo dei nuovi modelli di AI, in particolare di quelli più avanzati. Le incertezze intorno al futuro dell’azienda, a chi la dirigerà e al suo andamento in borsa potrebbero quindi avere effetti su un settore che è cresciuto molto velocemente, con poche regole e molti debiti, soprattutto negli Stati Uniti.

Oltre a vendere i processori più potenti disponibili sul mercato, Nvidia fornisce strumenti di sviluppo, reti ad alta velocità per collegare tra loro migliaia di processori e assistenza a chi costruisce i grandi data center per allenare e far funzionare i modelli AI più usati. Tra i suoi clienti ci sono OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta e Google, che spendono miliardi di dollari ogni anno per farsi concorrenza nello sviluppo dei cosiddetti modelli di frontiera, cioè i sistemi di intelligenza artificiale più avanzati e potenti.

Le loro spese enormi non sono per ora compensate dai ricavi, ma godono di grandi investimenti fatti da chi scommette sulle potenzialità delle AI per cambiare interi settori produttivi nei prossimi anni. La vicenda di Huang e le incertezze sulla sua successione dentro Nvidia potrebbero però cambiare il modo in cui gli investitori valutano le aziende delle AI. E questo potrebbe ritorcersi contro la stessa Nvidia.

Negli ultimi anni Huang aveva organizzato una parte importante delle attività di Nvidia intorno a meccanismi di “finanziamento circolare”, in cui l’azienda vende chip e al tempo stesso investe nell’ecosistema delle AI favorendo la domanda per i propri chip. Il caso più segnalato in questi giorni è quello di CoreWeave, una società statunitense che offre infrastrutture progettate intorno alle GPU ad alte prestazioni, cioè i sistemi di chip per l’addestramento e l’uso dei modelli di intelligenza artificiale.

CoreWeave acquista le GPU di Nvidia, le installa nei propri data center e vende poi la capacità di calcolo alle aziende. Nvidia possiede una partecipazione azionaria nella società di circa il 12 per cento. Quindi, da una parte vende i propri prodotti all’azienda, e dall’altra contribuisce a finanziarla, in modo che possa ingrandirsi e continuare ad acquistare le GPU.

Huang ha seguito il medesimo approccio con diverse altre aziende e si stima che Nvidia abbia ormai investito nell’ecosistema delle aziende di AI circa 99 miliardi di dollari. La società si è inoltre impegnata a partecipare a progetti da centinaia di miliardi di dollari per la costruzione di data center su larga scala, che servono a OpenAI e agli altri per sviluppare i loro modelli.

Grazie a questi accordi e agli avanzamenti tecnologici dei propri chip (in alcuni casi avanti di anni rispetto alla concorrenza), Nvidia ha creato nei fatti un monopolio nella fornitura delle GPU e degli altri sistemi. È avvenuto in particolare negli Stati Uniti, dove Huang ha gestito fitte relazioni personali con clienti, fornitori, partner tecnologici e politici, compreso il presidente Donald Trump. Finché il CEO di Nvidia aveva un’alta reputazione, e l’azienda non aveva difficoltà a soddisfare la domanda crescente di chip, poche società sembravano preoccuparsi più di tanto della loro forte dipendenza da un unico fornitore.

Questa condizione era però osservata da tempo dagli analisti che si occupano di capire se si sia formata una bolla finanziaria ed economica intorno alle AI, legata alla dubbia sostenibilità degli investimenti. Secondo molti di loro, Nvidia è diventata il perno intorno a cui ruota l’intero settore delle AI di frontiera negli Stati Uniti, con il rischio sempre più concreto che eventuali difficoltà dell’azienda si riflettano su tutto il resto.

Il confronto intorno alla “bolla delle AI” è ancora in corso e c’è chi intravede segnali di cedimento e altri che invece ritengono che i progressi nella tecnologia giustificheranno presto gli attuali investimenti. Al momento è difficile dire se Nvidia farà scoppiare questa bolla, ma di sicuro la vicenda di Huang ha contribuito a fare emergere la fragilità del settore.

Il consiglio di amministrazione di Nvidia è già alla ricerca del successore di Huang e ha interesse a trovare una soluzione in tempi rapidi, per ridurre l’incertezza e le perdite in borsa. La scelta di una persona affidabile, capace di rassicurare gli investitori e di rendere più trasparenti e meno personali i rapporti con i clienti rispetto a quanto facesse Huang, potrebbe rendere temporanea la crisi di Nvidia. Assorbito il danno finanziario e di reputazione, l’azienda potrebbe più o meno tornare a fare affari come prima, mantenendo la propria capacità commerciale e quella tecnologica.

La vicenda potrebbe però portare gli investitori a essere più prudenti e attenti, spingendo Nvidia a rivedere alcuni investimenti e finanziamenti, riducendo il proprio coinvolgimento diretto in alcuni dei progetti di sviluppo delle AI. I primi interessati da questa riduzione di flusso di denaro potrebbero essere gli operatori più piccoli, che avrebbero difficoltà a raccogliere capitali per costruire i loro data center. Il rallentamento degli investimenti avrebbe un impatto sull’intero settore, influendo sulle valutazioni delle aziende di intelligenza artificiale più grandi. Potrebbe essere un problema soprattutto per Anthropic, che ha nei piani di quotarsi a breve in borsa, e per OpenAI, che ha in programma di farlo il prossimo anno.

Nell’eventualità peggiore, secondo gli analisti, la riduzione degli investimenti si potrebbe combinare con una crescita dei ricavi inferiore alle aspettative. Diversi operatori non riuscirebbero più a ripagare i debiti o a rientrare delle spese per la costruzione dei data center, con una forte perdita di fiducia da parte degli investitori e ulteriori difficoltà a ottenere altro denaro. Questo rallentamento non porterebbe necessariamente alla fine delle AI, ma a un rallentamento nello sviluppo dei nuovi modelli. Per alcuni, gli effetti potrebbero essere positivi.

Come ha spiegato un analista ad Associated Press: «Tutto questo potrebbe trasformare in una gara aperta ciò che finora è stato nei fatti un monopolio». La domanda per i chip continua a esserci, ma potrebbe differenziarsi l’offerta, con maggiori possibilità per le aziende che li acquistano e con la costruzione di un settore con meno distorsioni e forti dipendenze da pochi soggetti. Nvidia in tutto questo potrebbe assistere a un ridimensionamento dei propri affari, e non solo sul mercato statunitense.

Gli Stati Uniti hanno imposto ormai da tempo limiti alle esportazioni dei chip più avanzati verso la Cina, per provare a conservare il proprio vantaggio tecnologico e militare. Il sospetto di un coinvolgimento di una spia cinese alla base della vicenda Nvidia potrebbe spingere il governo statunitense a estendere ulteriormente i controlli, occupandosi dei sistemi usati dalle aziende cinesi per acquistare direttamente le GPU Nvidia grazie a un intermediario, o sfruttandone le capacità di calcolo affittando data center in altre aree dell’Asia.

Reuters ha segnalato che alcune società cinesi stanno già provando a estendere il loro accesso alle GPU tramite data center all’estero, temendo l’arrivo di nuove limitazioni. I maggiori controlli potrebbero tradursi in minori opportunità di vendita per Nvidia e in una maggiore diversificazione del mercato, per quanto con chip meno potenti.

La presentazione dei dati dell’ultimo trimestre di Nvidia, prevista per il prossimo 17 novembre, sarà la prima opportunità per fare il punto sul mercato dei chip e delle AI. La società ha previsto ricavi per 108 miliardi di dollari, mentre gli analisti se ne aspettano 109, provenienti in buona parte dal settore dei data center. Sarebbe un aumento di oltre il 90 per cento rispetto all’anno scorso, ma poco indicativo per capire quanto a lungo potrà continuare una crescita a questi ritmi.

Difficilmente per il 17 novembre Nvidia avrà già un nuovo CEO e i dati saranno quindi presentati dalla direttrice finanziaria dell’azienda, Colette Kress, che ha ricevuto l’incarico di guida ad interim. Negli ultimi giorni sono circolate ipotesi su un ritorno di Huang, chiesto anche con una lettera aperta firmata da parte dei dipendenti di Nvidia. Nel settore delle AI le evoluzioni sono del resto veloci e imprevedibili.

Nel novembre del 2023 Sam Altman, il CEO di OpenAI, fu allontanato dalla guida dell’azienda e tornò al proprio posto dopo appena cinque giorni, anche grazie alle pressioni dei dipendenti e degli investitori. Altman non doveva però fare i conti con la possibilità di essere stato vittima di spionaggio e non aveva ricevuto un invito a testimoniare davanti al Congresso come Huang.

articles.body:
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.

The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.

Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.

The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.

The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.

It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.

“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.

But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.

“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.

Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.

Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.

I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.

But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.

His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot.

What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.

In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.

He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC.

Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.

“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”

“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.

“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.

It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.

But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.

That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.

Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.

But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load.

“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”

“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”

As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest.

In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.

It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.

But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia?

“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.”

Does Nvidia work without Huang?

Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.

“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”

“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”

“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.”

“Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.”

“No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang prima di tutto questo

articles.body:
Quella sua e di Nvidia è una storia cominciata in un ristorante popolare e arrivata dove non era arrivato nessuno

Il 26 settembre del 2023 Jensen Huang, uno degli uomini più potenti dell’industria tecnologica mondiale, era in un ristorante della catena Denny’s, un tipico diner popolare americano, nella città californiana di San Jose. Festeggiava i trent’anni di Nvidia, la più importante azienda di microchip statunitense, e il fatto che da poco aveva superato i mille miliardi di dollari di capitalizzazione. Era lì perché da ragazzo lavorava in un Denny’s, e proprio in quello di San Jose discusse per la prima volta di Nvidia con i due ingegneri Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem, con cui l’avrebbe poi fondata.

Quel ritorno da Denny’s dice molto del personaggio pubblico che Huang aveva costruito negli anni, prima che lo scandalo della sua relazione con una presunta spia cinese compromettesse irrimediabilmente la sua reputazione. Nella Silicon Valley Huang era un CEO estremamente riconoscibile, che partendo da un’infanzia difficile e un lavoro da lavapiatti era arrivato, passando attraverso varie crisi e fallimenti, a guidare l’azienda più strategica al mondo, e una delle più ricche.

Alla cerimonia indossava una giacca di pelle nera, come faceva ormai in quasi tutte le sue apparizioni pubbliche. Una volta, scherzando sull’immagine che si era costruito, si era presentato come «il tizio con la giacca di pelle che dice sempre le cose tre volte», ironizzando sulla sua tendenza a ripetere le cose importanti. Era una cosa che faceva spesso sia quando presentava i nuovi prodotti ai clienti, sia nelle frequenti riunioni interne all’azienda, in particolare quelle con i sessanta dirigenti che rispondevano direttamente a lui.

Tutta questa concentrazione di informazioni e potere aveva reso molto difficile immaginare Nvidia senza Huang, che infatti non aveva scelto un successore. Le rivelazioni sulle sue relazioni extraconiugali hanno però trasformato una vicenda privata in un problema di sicurezza nazionale e, dopo più di 33 anni alla guida dell’azienda, giovedì Huang si è dimesso ed è stato anche chiamato a testimoniare al Congresso.

Nelle sue dichiarazioni Huang si è definito orgoglioso e grato di essere un cittadino statunitense. La sua storia, d’altronde, è stata spesso descritta come un esempio di sogno americano che si realizza. Huang nacque a Taiwan nel 1963: a quel tempo l’isola era ancora sotto la legge marziale imposta dal presidente Chiang Kai-shek dopo la guerra civile con il Partito comunista cinese e stava appena cominciando la rapidissima trasformazione industriale che l’avrebbe resa una delle economie più avanzate dell’Asia. Quando aveva nove anni i genitori lo mandarono negli Stati Uniti insieme al fratello maggiore, da alcuni parenti.

Finirono tutti e due all’Oneida Baptist Institute, un collegio religioso del Kentucky rurale e che accoglieva ragazzi in situazioni difficili. Huang ha descritto quell’esperienza come una sorta di introduzione «hard knocks», «a bastonate», alla vita americana: ha raccontato che tutti gli studenti avevano delle mansioni (lui puliva i bagni del dormitorio dove dormivano circa 120 ragazzi), che molti studenti fumavano o portavano coltellini e che lui era stato bullizzato quasi tutti i giorni per il suo accento e per i suoi capelli lunghi.

Quando i genitori riuscirono a raggiungere lui e il fratello, la famiglia si trasferì in Oregon. A quindici anni Huang cominciò a lavorare in un Denny’s e a sedici si diplomò (partecipò anche alle competizioni di livello nazionale di tennistavolo). Si iscrisse alla facoltà di ingegneria elettronica della Oregon State University e lì conobbe Lori Mills, una delle poche studentesse della facoltà. Si sposarono cinque anni dopo, nel 1985, e poi ebbero due figli.

Nel frattempo nel 1984 Huang aveva iniziato a lavorare per alcune aziende di semiconduttori e lì incontrò due ingegneri, Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem. Loro lavoravano per un’azienda che progettava chip, e Huang per una che li produceva. Divennero amici e i due ingegneri proposero a Huang di fondare insieme una nuova azienda. Iniziarono a incontrarsi regolarmente da Denny’s perché lì si potevano bere tanti caffè e perché nessuno chiedeva loro di liberare il tavolo.

Decisero di iniziare a costruire processori per la grafica tridimensionale dei videogiochi. Inizialmente non avevano pensato a un nome per la loro azienda e quando dovettero registrarla ufficialmente cercarono qualcosa che contenesse le lettere “NV”, la sigla con cui salvavano i nomi di tutti i loro file di lavoro e che sta per next version, e cioè “prossima versione”. Scelsero così come nome “Nvidia”, dal latino invidia.

– Leggi anche: Quanto conta Jensen Huang per Nvidia

All’inizio le cose andarono molto male e Nvidia rischiò di fallire, ma riuscì a riprendersi con dei nuovi prodotti e un investimento della giapponese Sega. Nel 1999 si quotò in borsa e presentò la GeForce 256, il prodotto che contribuì a rendere popolare la sigla GPU (che sta per unità di elaborazione grafica). Come suggerisce il nome, le GPU erano state progettate per gestire le immagini dei videogiochi, ma riuscivano a svolgere moltissimi compiti contemporaneamente. Il loro potenziale insomma era enorme.

Nel 2006 Nvidia presentò CUDA, un insieme di strumenti che permetteva di usare le GPU anche per ambiti diversi dai videogiochi, con l’idea che ricercatori e sviluppatori trovassero nuovi modi di usarle. Ma fu soltanto sei anni dopo, nel 2012, che tre ricercatori mostrarono che una rete neurale, uno dei sistemi alla base delle moderne intelligenze artificiali, riusciva a ottenere risultati incredibili con CUDA e le GPU. Era la prima volta che Nvidia dimostrava di essere così efficace nel campo dell’AI, e Huang decise che ne avrebbe fatto la missione dell’azienda.

Nvidia cominciò a costruire prodotti sempre più specifici per queste applicazioni. Nel 2016 presentò DGX-1, un computer progettato appositamente per sviluppare sistemi di intelligenza artificiale, e il suo primo prototipo venne consegnato a OpenAI, l’azienda che avrebbe poi sviluppato ChatGPT. Nel 2017 realizzò Volta, una nuova generazione di processori con componenti progettati per accelerare i calcoli usati nelle reti neurali.

La domanda per i processori di Nvidia crebbe enormemente. Alle prestazioni eccezionali dei suoi chip si aggiungeva un vantaggio che i concorrenti facevano molta fatica a replicare: su CUDA e sulle GPU di Nvidia si erano accumulati anni di software, strumenti e competenze. Quando a partire dal 2022 ci fu la rapida ascesa dell’intelligenza artificiale generativa, quella di ChatGPT e Claude, Nvidia era già diventata indispensabile per lo sviluppo dei modelli più avanzati.

Intanto, sempre più governi avevano cominciato a considerare la capacità di costruire grandi sistemi di intelligenza artificiale una questione economica e strategica e avevano iniziato a fare accordi con Nvidia. Nel 2022, però, il governo statunitense decise di imporre delle restrizioni sulla vendita dei suoi chip più avanzati di Nvidia, sostenendo che potessero essere usati per scopi militari. Da quel momento sempre più decisioni commerciali di Nvidia iniziarono a passare direttamente dalle politiche di sicurezza nazionale americana, e viceversa Nvidia cominciò a influenzare le politiche pubbliche sull’AI.

Le restrizioni commerciali iniziarono però a farsi sempre più severe, e così Huang cominciò a fare pressione sull’amministrazione Biden. Insieme ad altri CEO sosteneva che limitare troppo l’accesso cinese ai chip americani avrebbe potuto ridurre i ricavi necessari alle aziende statunitensi per investire sulle nuove tecnologie, e spingere la Cina a sviluppare più rapidamente delle alternative proprie.

Huang aveva anche cominciato a promuovere quella che chiamava «sovereign AI», intelligenza artificiale sovrana, e cioè l’idea che ciascun paese dovesse sviluppare una propria AI: fece accordi con le aziende che le stavano sviluppando in molti paesi, come la saudita Humain e la Mistral francese.

La richiesta dei chip Nvidia continuava a crescere. Nell’anno fiscale 2024 Nvidia fatturò 60,9 miliardi di dollari, più del doppio dell’anno precedente. Huang ha raccontato di essersi fatto tatuare il logo di Nvidia, e di aver pianto un po’ mentre glielo facevano.

Huang era diventato anche uno dei maggiori sostenitori dei modelli di intelligenza artificiale aperti, e cioè quelli che chiunque può scaricare e adattare alle proprie esigenze. Era una strategia molto conveniente per Nvidia, perché più sono le persone che possono costruire e modificare modelli propri, più aumenta la domanda per i computer necessari ad addestrarli e farli funzionare.

Questa posizione sui modelli aperti era molto diversa da quella dell’amministrazione Biden, e molto in linea con quella di Trump. Nel suo piano nazionale sull’IA il governo trumpiano aveva dedicato un’intera sezione proprio ai modelli aperti: il rapporto sosteneva che favorissero lo sviluppo delle imprese e quindi la crescita economica statunitense. Sottolineava, inoltre, che avrebbero potuto diventare degli standard internazionali e quindi dare agli Stati Uniti anche un vantaggio geopolitico.

Anche per questo allineamento i rapporti tra Huang e Trump si erano fatti sempre più stretti: il 25 marzo Trump lo aveva nominato nel consiglio che dà indicazioni direttamente al presidente sulle politiche scientifiche e tecnologiche e a maggio lo aveva invitato personalmente ad accompagnarlo nella sua visita in Cina. Secondo il New York Times, Trump sapeva della relazione di Huang con la presunta spia cinese Alice Huang già dal 2025.

articles.body:
La carrera por presidir el Banco Central Europeo parece un sprint, pero aún no ha terminado, y se ha parecido más a una maratón, por más que los acontecimientos se hayan sucedido a velocidad de vértigo. El pasado 29 de octubre, la presidenta Christine Lagarde anunciaba su dimisión, efectiva el 7 de febrero. Este viernes, dos semanas después, el canciller alemán Friedrich Merz anunciaba que el acuerdo final es cuestión de días .

A fecha de hoy, el favorito cada vez más claro es el español Pablo Hernández de Cos, director gerente del Banco Internacional de Pagos de Basilea y exgobernador del Banco de España, por delante del otro candidato oficial, el holandés Klaas Knot. Aunque, como advertía el líder alemán, Friedrich Merz, en Dublín este mismo viernes: “Las conversaciones tampoco han concluido todavía”. Y eso quiere decir que, en el poco tiempo que falta para adoptar decisión, el escenario puede cambiar.

articles.body:
La conclusione del Pnrr apre un’incognita sulla fine del 2026. Intanto nei primi mesi dell’anno le esportazioni crescono del 15%: nonostante questo l’industria sconta una certa debolezza legata all’incertezza del contesto e alle prospettive dell’ex-Ilva

In Puglia export aumentato del 15% e Pil regionale dell’1%, complici gli investimenti del Pnrr. I dati del rapporto congiunturale di Bankitalia si riferiscono al primo semestre dell’anno, rispetto allo stesso periodo del 2025 e sono in linea con quelli dell’Italia e del Sud, rispettivamente pari allo 0,9 e all’1%. La seconda parte dell’anno - si legge nel rapporto - prefigura invece un peggioramento, per effetto della conclusione del Pnrr, dell’aumento dell’inflazione, delle tensioni internazionali e dell’incertezza sul futuro della ex-Ilva.

Se la domanda interna è cresciuta in misura contenuta con un incremento moderato dei consumi e un andamento debole degli investimenti, la domanda estera si è invece rafforzata con una performance a doppia cifra. L’industria ha mostrato una crescita modesta - nonostante il forte recupero delle esportazioni - a causa dell’incertezza legata, appunto, alle prospettive dell’ex-Ilva. L’espansione è stata più intensa nel settore delle costruzioni, in particolare nelle opere pubbliche, e così nel terziario con l’andamento favorevole delle attività turistico-ricettive caratterizzate da una particolare incidenza di lavoro part time e stagionale, oltre che da un complessivo non alto valore aggiunto sull’economia regionale.

Quanto al Pnrr, i pagamenti in Puglia, a giugno 2026, sono stati pari a 5,7 miliardi di euro, il 54% delle risorse previste, a fronte di circa 4,4 miliardi dello scorso aprile. Rispetto al dato nazionale, la progressione è inferiore alla media italiana in tutte le missioni ed è più accentuata nella missione 3 “Infrastrutture per una mobilità sostenibile”.

Nel primo semestre del 2026 l’occupazione è risalita dello 0,6%, dopo il lieve calo del 2025, mentre ad aumentare è stato in particolare quello autonomo(1,9%). Il tasso di occupazione è cresciuto dello 0,7%, al 51,7%, e il divario con l’Italia è rimasto sostanzialmente invariato a 11,3 punti.

«La ripresa - spiega Marcello Malamisura, direttore della sede di Bari di Bankitalia - si è associata però ad un ulteriore incremento della diffusione degli ammortizzatori sociali, che resta più elevata rispetto alla media nazionale anche per il perdurare di alcune importanti crisi aziendali, tra cui quella del polo siderurgico tarantino». Il potere d’acquisto è aumentato in misura contenuta: l’espansione si è concentrata nei primi 3 mesi diventando lievemente negativa nel secondo trimestre, a causa del rialzo dell’inflazione. Per quanto riguarda, invece, i finanziamenti alle famiglie, hanno continuato a crescere con intensità simile a quella della fine dello scorso anno: all’accelerazione del credito al consumo si è contrapposto il rallentamento dei mutui per l’acquisto di abitazioni.

articles.title: China, US discuss tariffs, farm trade at first trade council meeting

BEIJING: China and the United States discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at their first trade council meeting on Friday (Nov 13), China's Commerce Ministry said on Saturday, days ahead of an expected leaders' meeting in Shenzhen next week.
articles.body:
China's commerce ministry did not say whether any agreements were reached, only that both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues.

BEIJING: China and the United States discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at their first trade council meeting on Friday (Nov 13), China's Commerce Ministry said on Saturday, days ahead of an expected leaders' meeting in Shenzhen next week.

"The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the outcomes of previous China-US economic and trade talks, including tariffs, a reciprocal 'US$30 billion-for-US$30 billion' tariff-cut arrangement, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern," the ministry said.

It did not say whether any agreements were reached. Both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues, the ministry added.

Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, but the plan has yet to be finalised.

Chinese purchases of US farm goods other than soybeans are on track to hit a seven-year low this year, despite an agreement to buy US$17 billion annually through 2028, a Reuters analysis of customs data showed earlier this month, underscoring persistent uncertainty over the deal.

Beijing has repeatedly urged Washington to implement the US$60 billion tariff-reduction deal, calling it a prerequisite for increasing purchases of US farm goods.

The White House said Trump will meet Xi on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen.
